title: Mitosis and the Cell Cycle
subtitle: How somatic cells copy themselves without changing the code
subject: Biology
syllabusModule: Module 5 Heredity (2017) + Cells as the basis of life (2025)
syllabusDotPoints: model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to: mitosis and meiosis (ACSBL075)
assess the effect of the cell replication processes on the continuity of species (ACSBL084)
Account for the phases of gap 1 (G1), synthesis, gap 2 (G2) and mitosis in the cell cycle
Compare the structures and roles of somatic and gametic cells
Conduct a practical investigation to model the named phases of mitosis and cytokinesis
inquiryQuestion: How important is it for genetic material to be replicated exactly?
lessonIntent: Students can account for the G1, S, G2 and M phases of the cell cycle, sequence mitosis and cytokinesis, compare somatic and gametic cells, and explain how mitosis maintains chromosome number.
examSkill: Sequence the cell cycle and the stages of mitosis, track chromosome number through division, and compare somatic and gametic cells.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, the cell cycle and mitosis. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: The cells that never stopped dividing
scenes.body: HeLa cells, taken in 1951, are still dividing in labs more than 70 years later. Their cell cycle controls are broken.
scenes.callout: What normally tells a cell when to copy its DNA and divide?
scenes.caption: HeLa cells divide without limit because their cell cycle control is broken.

voiceover.text: In nineteen fifty one, cancer cells taken from a patient named Henrietta Lacks were grown in a dish, and astonishingly, they just kept dividing. Those cells, now called HeLa, are still dividing in labs more than seventy years later, and they helped test the first polio vaccine. Normal body cells don't behave like that. They grow, copy their DNA and divide in a controlled sequence called the cell cycle, and in cancer cells like HeLa that control has broken down. So today's question is, what does a normal cell do in each stage of that cycle, and how does mitosis copy a cell while keeping its chromosomes the same?

scenes.heading: The cell cycle: G1, S, G2, then M
scenes.body: Interphase (G1, S and G2) prepares the cell; the M phase divides it.

bullets.text: G1 (gap 1): the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and does its normal job.
S (synthesis): DNA replicates, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids.
G2 (gap 2): more growth, and the cell checks its DNA and prepares to divide.
M phase: mitosis divides the nucleus, then cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

scenes.callout: Copy first, in S. Divide later, in M.
scenes.caption: G1 growth, S phase DNA replication, G2 preparation, then mitosis and cytokinesis.

voiceover.text: OK, let's map out the cell cycle, because mitosis is only one short part of it. Most of a cell's life is spent in interphase, which has three phases. First is G1, which stands for gap one. The cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and gets on with its normal job. Then comes S, the synthesis phase, where the cell replicates all of its DNA, using the semiconservative process we have already covered. By the end of S, each chromosome is two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere. Next is G2, gap two, where the cell keeps growing, makes the proteins it needs for division, and checks that its DNA was copied correctly. Only then does the cell enter M phase, where mitosis divides the nucleus and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. So the rule is copy first, in S, and divide later, in M.

scenes.heading: Mitosis, then cytokinesis
scenes.body: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase separate the chromatids; cytokinesis splits the cell.

bullets.text: Prophase: chromosomes condense and the nuclear membrane breaks down.
Metaphase: chromosomes line up along the cell's equator on the spindle.
Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
Telophase: a new nuclear membrane forms around each set of chromosomes.
Cytokinesis: a cleavage furrow (animals) or cell plate (plants) splits the cell in two.

scenes.secondary: The two daughter cells end with the same chromosome number as the parent.
scenes.callout: Condense, align, separate, rebuild, split. Same number out as in.
scenes.caption: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis give two cells with the parent's chromosome number.

voiceover.text: Now the division itself. Mitosis runs in four stages, and you need them in order. In prophase, the chromosomes, already copied into sister chromatids, condense and become visible, and the nuclear membrane breaks down. In metaphase, the chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres. Anaphase is the dramatic one, where the sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles of the cell. And in telophase, a new nuclear membrane forms around each set of chromosomes. Then cytokinesis finishes the job by dividing the cytoplasm. In animal cells the membrane pinches inwards to form a cleavage furrow, while plant cells build a cell plate that becomes the new cell wall. The outcome is two daughter cells, each with the same chromosome number as the parent.

scenes.heading: Somatic cells vs gametic cells
scenes.body: Somatic cells are body cells made by mitosis; gametic cells are sex cells made by meiosis.

bullets.text: Somatic cells: body cells, diploid (46 chromosomes in humans), made by mitosis for growth and repair.
Gametic cells: sperm and eggs, haploid (23 in humans), made by meiosis for fertilisation.
A mutation in a somatic cell is not passed to offspring; one in a gamete can be.

scenes.callout: Mitosis keeps somatic cells stable; gametes carry DNA to the next generation.
scenes.caption: Somatic cells are diploid body cells made by mitosis; gametes are haploid sex cells made by meiosis.

voiceover.text: So which cells does mitosis actually make? That brings us to a comparison you need, somatic cells versus gametic cells. Somatic cells are body cells, like skin, muscle and liver cells. In humans they're diploid, with forty six chromosomes in two sets, and they're made by mitosis, which is why they keep a stable chromosome number for growth, repair and everyday function. Gametic cells, or gametes, are the sex cells, sperm and eggs. They're haploid, with just twenty three chromosomes, one set, and they're made by meiosis. Their structures suit their role in fertilisation, so a sperm has a flagellum to swim, and an egg is large, with a food store for the early embryo. Here's why the difference matters. A mutation in a somatic cell stays in that body, but a mutation in a gamete can be passed on to the next generation.

rows: Sperm: flagellum. Egg: large, food store

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Cell cycle: the sequence of G1, S, G2 and M phases a cell passes through to divide.
Interphase: G1, S and G2, when the cell grows and copies its DNA.
Sister chromatids: two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at a centromere.
Mitosis: nuclear division giving two nuclei with the parent's chromosome number.
Cytokinesis: division of the cytoplasm into two separate daughter cells.

scenes.callout: These five terms describe faithful copying, not variation.
scenes.caption: Cell cycle, interphase, sister chromatids, mitosis and cytokinesis defined.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the vocabulary. The cell cycle is the sequence of G1, S, G2 and M phases that a cell passes through to divide. Interphase covers G1, S and G2, the time when the cell grows and copies its DNA. Sister chromatids are the two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere, which is why a copied chromosome looks like an X. Mitosis is the division of the nucleus, giving two nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent. And cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm, which physically splits the cell into two daughter cells. Notice that every one of these terms is about faithful copying, not about creating anything new.

scenes.heading: Track the chromosome number
scenes.question: A human somatic cell with 46 chromosomes goes through one cell cycle. State the chromosome number in each daughter cell, and identify the phase in which the DNA was copied.
scenes.coachNote: DNA is copied in S phase, before mitosis. Do not halve the number; mitosis keeps it constant.
steps: In S phase of interphase, the cell replicates its DNA, so each of the 46 chromosomes becomes two sister chromatids.
In anaphase, sister chromatids separate, sending one full set to each pole.
After telophase and cytokinesis, each daughter cell has 46 chromosomes, the same as the parent.
Mitosis maintains chromosome number; halving it is what meiosis does.
Answer: 46 chromosomes in each daughter cell; the DNA was copied in S phase.
scenes.caption: Each daughter cell has 46 chromosomes; DNA was copied in S phase, before mitosis.

voiceover.text: Let's track the chromosome number, because students lose marks by halving it. A human somatic cell with forty six chromosomes goes through one cell cycle. State the chromosome number in each daughter cell, and identify when the DNA was copied. Step one, in the S phase of interphase, the cell replicates its DNA, so each of the forty six chromosomes becomes two sister chromatids. Step two, in anaphase, those sister chromatids separate, sending one complete set to each pole. Step three, after telophase and cytokinesis, each daughter cell has forty six chromosomes, exactly the same as the parent. Mitosis maintains the number, and halving it is what meiosis does. So the answer is forty six chromosomes in each daughter cell, with the DNA copied in S phase, not during mitosis.

scenes.heading: Two mitosis traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking mitosis produces genetically different daughter cells. It produces cells genetically identical to each other and the parent; variation comes from meiosis.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: thinking mitosis only happens during early growth. It continues throughout life in renewing tissues like skin, gut lining and blood, and in wound repair. Neurons and heart muscle cells rarely divide, which is why that damage is hard to repair.
scenes.callout: Mitosis is for identical copies, and it runs all life long.
scenes.caption: Mitosis makes identical cells, not variation, and continues throughout life in renewing tissues.

voiceover.text: Two traps on mitosis. Trap one, thinking that mitosis produces genetically different daughter cells. It's the opposite. Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to each other and to the parent, barring the occasional copying error. Variation comes from meiosis, so never credit mitosis with creating it. Trap two, thinking mitosis only happens while you're growing up. Not true. It continues throughout life in tissues that keep renewing, like your skin, the lining of your gut and the cells that make your blood, and of course in wound repair. The flip side is that some cells, like neurons and heart muscle cells, rarely divide, which is why damage to the brain or heart is so hard to repair.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A skin wound heals by producing many new cells to replace damaged ones. Explain why mitosis, rather than meiosis, is the appropriate division, referring to chromosome number and genetic stability.
answerSteps: Wound repair needs new cells genetically identical to the skin cells being replaced.
Mitosis produces daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent, keeping them functional skin cells.
It maintains genetic stability, so the new cells behave just like the originals.
Meiosis would halve the chromosome number and create variation, useless for replacing body cells.
Answer: mitosis is correct because it keeps chromosome number and genetic information stable for like-for-like repair.
scenes.caption: Wound repair needs mitosis: identical cells with stable chromosome number, not meiosis.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A skin wound heals by producing many new cells to replace the damaged ones. Explain why mitosis, rather than meiosis, is the right division here, referring to chromosome number and genetic stability. Pause and reason it through. Right. Healing a wound needs new cells that are genetically identical to the skin cells being replaced, so you want exact replacements, not something different. Mitosis delivers that, because it produces somatic cells with the same chromosome number as the parent, so they stay fully functional skin cells. It also maintains genetic stability, meaning the new cells carry the same information and behave just like the originals. Meiosis would halve the chromosome number and create variation, which is exactly what you don't want when replacing body cells. So mitosis is correct because it keeps the chromosome number and the genetic information stable, giving you like for like repair.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Cell cycle: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation), then M (mitosis and cytokinesis).
Mitosis in order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis.
Daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent and are genetically identical.
Somatic cells are diploid body cells made by mitosis; gametes are haploid and made by meiosis.
Mitosis is for growth and repair, does not create variation, and continues throughout life.
scenes.finalPrompt: Mitosis question? Copy in S, divide in M, and the chromosome number stays the same.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: the cell cycle, the stages, stable number, somatic vs gametic cells, the role of mitosis.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five takeaways. First, the cell cycle runs G1 for growth, S for DNA replication, G2 for preparation, then M for mitosis and cytokinesis. Second, mitosis goes prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, and cytokinesis then splits the cell. Third, the daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent and are genetically identical to it. Fourth, somatic cells are diploid body cells made by mitosis, while gametes are haploid sex cells made by meiosis. And fifth, mitosis is for growth and repair, it doesn't create variation, and it keeps running all your life. So remember the rhythm, copy in S, divide in M, and the number stays the same. Next up, meiosis, the division that halves the number and creates variation.
